{{short description|Continued fraction closely related to the Rogers–Ramanujan identities}}
The '''Rogers–Ramanujan continued fraction'''  is a [[continued fraction]] discovered by   {{harvtxt|Rogers|1894}} and independently by [[Srinivasa Ramanujan]], and closely related to the [[Rogers–Ramanujan identities]]. It can be evaluated explicitly for a broad class of values of its argument.
[[File:Rogers400.png|right|thumb|[[Domain coloring]] representation of the convergent <math> A_{400}(q)/B_{400}(q)</math> of  the function <math> q^{-1/5}R(q)</math>, where <math> R(q)</math> is the Rogers–Ramanujan continued fraction.]]

==Definition==
[[File:RogersRamanujan400.png|right|thumb|Representation of the approximation  <math> q^{1/5}A_{400}(q)/B_{400}(q)</math> of the Rogers–Ramanujan continued fraction.]]

Given the functions <math>G(q)</math> and <math>H(q)</math> appearing in the Rogers–Ramanujan identities, and assume <math>q=e^{2\pi i \tau}</math>,

:<math>\begin{align}G(q)
&= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac {q^{n^2}} {(1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots(1-q^n)} =\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac {q^{n^2}} {(q;q)_n} = \frac {1}{(q;q^5)_\infty (q^4; q^5)_\infty}\\[6pt]
&= \prod_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(1-q^{5n-1})(1-q^{5n-4})}\\[6pt]
&=\sqrt[60]{q\,j}\,\,_2F_1\left(-\tfrac{1}{60},\tfrac{19}{60};\tfrac{4}{5};\tfrac{1728}{j}\right)\\[6pt]
&=\sqrt[60]{q\left(j-1728\right)}\,_2F_1\left(-\tfrac{1}{60},\tfrac{29}{60};\tfrac{4}{5};-\tfrac{1728}{j-1728}\right)\\[6pt]
&= 1+ q +q^2 +q^3 +2q^4+2q^5 +3q^6+\cdots
\end{align}</math>

and,

:<math>\begin{align}H(q)
&= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac {q^{n^2+n}} {(1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots(1-q^n)}  =\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac {q^{n^2+n}} {(q;q)_n} = \frac {1}{(q^2;q^5)_\infty (q^3; q^5)_\infty}\\[6pt]
&= \prod_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(1-q^{5n-2})(1-q^{5n-3})}\\[6pt]
&=\frac{1}{\sqrt[60]{q^{11}j^{11}}}\,_2F_1\left(\tfrac{11}{60},\tfrac{31}{60};\tfrac{6}{5};\tfrac{1728}{j}\right)\\[6pt]
&=\frac{1}{\sqrt[60]{q^{11}\left(j-1728\right)^{11}}}\,_2F_1\left(\tfrac{11}{60},\tfrac{41}{60};\tfrac{6}{5};-\tfrac{1728}{j-1728}\right)\\[6pt]
&= 1+q^2 +q^3 +q^4+q^5 +2q^6+2q^7+\cdots
\end{align}</math>

with the coefficients of the ''q''-expansion being {{OEIS2C|id=A003114}} and {{OEIS2C|id=A003106}}, respectively, where <math>(a;q)_\infty</math> denotes the infinite [[q-Pochhammer symbol]], ''j'' is the [[j-invariant|j-function]], and <sub>2</sub>F<sub>1</sub> is the [[hypergeometric function]]. The Rogers–Ramanujan continued fraction is then

:<math>\begin{align}R(q)
&= \frac{q^{\frac{11}{60}}H(q)}{q^{-\frac{1}{60}}G(q)} = q^{\frac{1}{5}}\prod_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(1-q^{5n-1})(1-q^{5n-4})}{(1-q^{5n-2})(1-q^{5n-3})}=q^{1/5}\prod^{\infty}_{n=1}(1-q^n)^{(n|5)} \\[8pt]
&= \cfrac{q^{1/5}}{1+\cfrac{q}{1+\cfrac{q^2}{1+\cfrac{q^3}{1+\ddots}}}}
\end{align}</math>
:<math>(n\mid m)</math> is the [[Jacobi symbol]].

One should be careful with notation since the formulas employing the [[j-invariant|j-function]] <math>j</math> will be consistent with the other formulas only if <math>q=e^{2\pi i \tau}</math> (the square of the [[nome (mathematics)|nome]]) is used throughout this section since the ''q''-expansion of the j-function (as well as the well-known [[Dedekind eta function]]) uses <math>q=e^{2\pi i \tau}</math>. However, Ramanujan, in his examples to Hardy and given below, used the ''nome'' <math>q=e^{\pi i \tau}</math>instead.{{cn|date=April 2022}}

==Special values==
If ''q'' is the [[nome (mathematics)|nome]] or its square, then <math>q^{-\frac{1}{60}}G(q)</math> and <math>q^{\frac{11}{60}}H(q)</math>, as well as their quotient <math>R(q)</math>, are related to [[modular function]]s of <math>\tau</math>. Since they have integral coefficients, the theory of [[complex multiplication]] implies that their values for <math>\tau</math> involving an imaginary quadratic field are [[algebraic number]]s that can be evaluated explicitly.

===Examples of R(q)===

Given the general form where Ramanujan used the [[nome (mathematics)|nome]] <math>q = e^{\pi i \tau}</math>,

:<math>R(q) = \cfrac{q^{1/5}}{1+\cfrac{q}{1+\cfrac{q^2}{1+\cfrac{q^3}{1+\ddots}}}}</math>
f
when <math>\tau = i</math>,

:<math>R\big(e^{-\pi}\big) = \cfrac{e^{-\frac{\pi}{5}}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-\pi}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-2\pi}}{1+\ddots}}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\varphi\,(\sqrt{5}-\varphi^{3/2})(\sqrt[4]{5}+\varphi^{3/2}) = 0.511428\dots</math>

when <math>\tau = 2i</math>,

:<math>R\big(e^{-2\pi}\big) = \cfrac{e^{-\frac{2\pi}{5}}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-2\pi}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-4\pi}}{1+\ddots}}} = {\sqrt[4]{5}\,\varphi^{1/2}-\varphi} = 0.284079\dots</math>

when <math>\tau = 4i</math>,

:<math>R\big(e^{-4\pi}\big) = \cfrac{e^{-\frac{4\pi}{5}}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-4\pi}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-8\pi}}{1+\ddots}}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\varphi\,(\sqrt{5}-\varphi^{3/2})(-\sqrt[4]{5}+\varphi^{3/2}) = 0.081002\dots</math>

when <math>\tau = 2\sqrt{5}i</math>,

:<math>R\big(e^{-2\sqrt{5}\pi}\big) = \cfrac{e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt5}}}{1+\cfrac{e^{-2\pi\sqrt{5}}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-4\pi\sqrt{5}}}{1+\ddots}}} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{1+\big(5^{3/4} (\varphi-1)^{5/2}-1\big)^{1/5}} - \varphi = 0.0602094\dots</math>

when <math>\tau = 5i</math>,

:<math>R\big(e^{-5\pi}\big) = \cfrac{e^{-\pi}}{1+\cfrac{e^{-5\pi}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-10\pi}}{1+\ddots}}} = \frac{1+\varphi^2}{\varphi+\big(\frac{1}{2}(4-\varphi-3\sqrt{\varphi-1})(3\varphi^{3/2}-\sqrt[4]{5})\big)^{1/5}} - \varphi = 0.0432139\dots</math>

when <math>\tau = 10i</math>,

:<math>R\big(e^{-10\pi}\big) = \cfrac{e^{-2\pi}}{1+\cfrac{e^{-10\pi}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-20\pi}}{1+\ddots}}} = \frac{1+\varphi^2}{\varphi+\big(3\sqrt{1+\varphi^2}-4-\varphi\big)^{1/5}} - \varphi = 0.00186744\dots</math>

when <math>\tau = 20i</math>,

:<math>R\big(e^{-20\pi}\big) = \cfrac{e^{-4\pi}}{1+\cfrac{e^{-20\pi}}{1 + \cfrac{e^{-40\pi}}{1+\ddots}}} = \frac{1+\varphi^2}{\varphi+\big(\frac{1}{2}(4-\varphi-3\sqrt{\varphi-1})(3\varphi^{3/2}+\sqrt[4]{5})\big)^{1/5}} - \varphi = 0.00000348734\dots</math>

and <math>\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}</math> is the [[golden ratio]]. Note that <math>R\big(e^{-2\pi}\big)</math> is a positive root of the [[quartic equation]],

:<math>x^4+2x^3-6x^2-2x+1=0</math>

while <math>R\big(e^{-\pi}\big)</math> and <math>R\big(e^{-4\pi}\big)</math> are two positive roots of a single [[octic]],

:<math>y^4+2\varphi^4 y^3+6\varphi^2 y^2-2\varphi^4 y+1=0</math>

(since <math>\varphi</math> has a square root) which explains the similarity of the two closed-forms. More generally, for positive [[integer]] ''m'', then <math>R(e^{-2\pi/m})</math> and <math>R(e^{-2\pi\, m})</math> are two roots of the same equation as well as,

:<math>\bigl[R(e^{-2\pi/m}) +\varphi\bigr] \bigl[R(e^{-2\pi\, m}) +\varphi\bigr] = \sqrt5\,\varphi</math>

The algebraic degree ''k'' of <math>R(e^{-\pi\, n})</math> for <math>n = 1,2,3,4,\dots</math> is <math>k = 8,4,32,8,\dots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A082682}}).

Incidentally, these continued fractions can be used to solve some [[quintic function|quintic equations]] as shown in a later section.

===Examples of ''G''(''q'') and ''H''(''q'')===

Interestingly, there are explicit formulas for <math>G(q)</math> and <math>H(q)</math> in terms of the [[j-invariant|j-function]] <math>j(\tau)</math> and the Rogers-Ramanujan continued fraction <math>R(q)</math>. However, since <math>j(\tau)</math> uses the nome's square <math>q = e^{2\pi\,i\tau}</math>, then one should be careful with notation such that <math>j(\tau),\,G(q),\, H(q)</math> and <math>r = R(q)</math> use the same <math>q</math>.

:<math>\begin{align}
G(q) &= \prod_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(1-q^{5n-1})(1-q^{5n-4})}\\[6pt]
&= q^{1/60} \frac{j(\tau)^{1/60}}{(r^{20}-228r^{15}+494r^{10}+228r^5+1)^{1/20}}
\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}
H(q) &= \prod_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(1-q^{5n-2})(1-q^{5n-3})}\\[6pt]
&= \frac{-1}{q^{11/60}} \frac{(r^{20}-228r^{15}+494r^{10}+228r^5+1)^{11/20}}{j(\tau)^{11/60}\,(r^{10}+11r^5-1)}
\end{align}</math>

Of course, the secondary formulas imply that <math>q^{-1/60}G(q)</math> and <math>q^{11/60}H(q)</math> are [[algebraic numbers]] (though normally of high degree) for <math>\tau</math> involving an [[imaginary quadratic field]]. For example, the formulas above simplify to,

:<math>\begin{align}
G(e^{-2\pi})
&= (e^{-2\pi})^{1/60} \frac1{(5\,\varphi)^{1/4}} \frac1{\sqrt{ R(e^{-2\pi}) }} \\[6pt]
&= 1.00187093\dots\\[6pt]
H(e^{-2\pi})
&= \frac1{(e^{-2\pi})^{11/60}} \frac1{(5\,\varphi)^{1/4}} \sqrt{ R(e^{-2\pi}) } \\[6pt]
&= 1.00000349\ldots
\end{align}</math>

and,

:<math>\begin{align}
G(e^{-4\pi})
&= (e^{-4\pi})^{1/60} \frac1{(5\,\varphi^3)^{1/4}\,(\varphi+\sqrt[4]{5})^{1/4}} \frac1{\sqrt{ R(e^{-4\pi}) }} \\[6pt]
&= 1.000003487354\dots\\[6pt]
H(e^{-4\pi})
&= \frac1{(e^{-4\pi})^{11/60}} \frac1{(5\,\varphi^3)^{1/4}\,(\varphi+\sqrt[4]{5})^{1/4}} \sqrt{ R(e^{-4\pi}) } \\[6pt]
&= 1.000000000012\dots
\end{align}</math>

and so on, with <math>\varphi</math> as the golden ratio.

== Derivation of special values ==

=== Tangential sums ===

In the following we express the essential theorems of the Rogers-Ramanujan continued fractions R and S by using the [[List of trigonometric identities#Angle sum and difference identities|tangential sums]] and tangential differences:

:<math> a \oplus b = \tan\bigl[\arctan(a) + \arctan(b)\bigr] = \frac{a + b}{1 - ab} </math>

:<math> c \ominus d = \tan\bigl[\arctan(c) - \arctan(d)\bigr] = \frac{c - d}{1 + cd} </math>

The [[nome (mathematics)|elliptic nome]] and the ''complementary nome'' have this relationship to each other:

:<math> \ln(q) \ln(q_{1}) = \pi^2 </math>

The complementary nome of a modulus k is equal to the nome of the Pythagorean complementary modulus:

:<math> q_{1}(k) = q(k') = q(\sqrt{1 - k^2}) </math>

These are the reflection theorems for the continued fractions R and S:

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math> S(q) \oplus S(q_1)= \Phi </math>
|-
|<math> R(q^2) \oplus R(q_1^2)= \Phi^{-1} </math>
|}

The letter <math> \Phi </math> represents the [[Golden ratio|Golden number]] exactly:

:<math> \Phi = \tfrac{1}{2}(\sqrt{5} + 1) = \cot[\tfrac{1}{2}\arctan(2)] = 2\cos(\tfrac{1}{5}{\pi}) </math>

:<math> \Phi^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\sqrt{5} - 1) = \tan[\tfrac{1}{2}\arctan(2)] = 2\sin(\tfrac{1}{10}{\pi}) </math>

The theorems for the squared nome are constructed as follows:

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math> R(q)^2 R(q^2)^{-1}\oplus R(q)R(q^2)^2 =1 </math>
|-
|<math> S(q)^2 R(q^2)^{-1}\ominus S(q)R(q^2)^2 =1 </math>
|}

Following relations between the continued fractions and the Jacobi theta functions are given:

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math> S(q) \oplus R(q^2) = \frac{\vartheta_{00}(q^{1/5})^2 - \vartheta_{00}(q)^2}{5\,\vartheta_{00}(q^5)^2 - \vartheta_{00}(q)^2} </math>
|-
|<math> R(q) \ominus R(q^2) = \frac{\vartheta_{01}(q)^2 - \vartheta_{01}(q^{1/5})^2}{5\,\vartheta_{01}(q^5)^2 - \vartheta_{01}(q)^2} </math>
|}

=== Derivation of Lemniscatic values ===

Into the now shown theorems certain values are inserted:

:<math> S\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] \oplus S\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] = \Phi </math>

Therefore following identity is valid:

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math> S\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{2}\arctan(\Phi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{4}\pi - \tfrac{1}{4}\arctan(2)\bigr] </math>
|}

In an analogue pattern we get this result:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-2\pi)\bigr] \oplus R\bigl[\exp(-2\pi)\bigr] = \Phi^{-1} </math>

Therefore following identity is valid:

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math> R\bigl[\exp(-2\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{2}\arctan(\Phi^{-1})\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{4}\arctan(2)\bigr] </math>
|}

Furthermore we get the same relation by using the above mentioned theorem about the Jacobi theta functions:

:<math> S\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] \oplus R\bigl[\exp(-2\pi)\bigr] = S(q) \oplus R(q^2) \bigl[q = \exp(-\pi)\bigr] = </math>

:<math> = \frac{\vartheta_{00}(q^{1/5})^2 - \vartheta_{00}(q)^2}{5\,\vartheta_{00}(q^5)^2 - \vartheta_{00}(q)^2} \bigl[q = \exp(-\pi)\bigr] = 1 </math>

This result appears because of the [[Poisson summation formula]] and this equation can be solved in this way:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-2\pi)\bigr] = 1 \ominus S\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] = 1 \ominus \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{4}\pi - \tfrac{1}{4}\arctan(2)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{4}\arctan(2)\bigr] </math>

By taking the other mentioned theorem about the Jacobi theta functions a next value can be determined:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] \ominus R\bigl[\exp(-2\pi)\bigr] = R(q) \ominus R(q^2) \bigl[q = \exp(-\pi)\bigr] = </math>

:<math> = \frac{\vartheta_{01}(q)^2 - \vartheta_{01}(q^{1/5})^2}{5\,\vartheta_{01}(q^5)^2 - \vartheta_{01}(q)^2} \bigl[q = \exp(-\pi)\bigr] = \frac{\sqrt[4]{5} - 1}{\sqrt[4]{5} + 1} = \sqrt[4]{5} \ominus 1 = \tan\bigl[\arctan(\sqrt[4]{5}\,) - \tfrac{1}{4}\pi \bigr] </math>

That equation chain leads to this tangential sum:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] = R\bigl[\exp(-2\pi)\bigr] \oplus \tan\bigl[\arctan(\sqrt[4]{5}\,) - \tfrac{1}{4}\pi \bigr] </math>

And therefore following result appears:

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{4}\arctan(2) + \arctan(\sqrt[4]{5}\,) - \tfrac{1}{4}\pi \bigr] </math>
|}

In the next step we use the [[reflection theorem]] for the continued fraction R again:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] \oplus R\bigl[\exp(-4\pi)\bigr] = \Phi^{-1} </math>

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-4\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{2}\arctan(2)\bigr] \ominus R\bigl[\exp(-\pi)\bigr] </math>

And a further result appears:

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math> R\bigl[\exp(-4\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{4}\arctan(2) - \arctan(\sqrt[4]{5}\,) + \tfrac{1}{4}\pi \bigr] </math>
|}

=== Derivation of Non-Lemniscatic values ===

The reflection theorem is now used for following values:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] \oplus R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \Phi^{-1} </math>

The Jacobi theta theorem leads to a further relation:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] \ominus R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = R(q) \ominus R(q^2) \bigl[q = \exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = </math>

:<math> = \frac{\vartheta_{01}(q)^2 - \vartheta_{01}(q^{1/5})^2}{5\,\vartheta_{01}(q^5)^2 - \vartheta_{01}(q)^2} \bigl[q = \exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[2\arctan(\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{5} - \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} + 4\sqrt{5}} + \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} - 4\sqrt{5}}\,) - \tfrac{1}{4}\pi \bigr] </math>

By tangential adding the now mentioned two theorems we get this result:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] \oplus R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \Phi^{-1} \oplus \tan\bigl[2\arctan(\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{5} - \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} + 4\sqrt{5}} + \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} - 4\sqrt{5}}\,) - \tfrac{1}{4}\pi \bigr] </math>

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math>R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\arctan(\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{5} - \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} + 4\sqrt{5}} + \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} - 4\sqrt{5}}\,) - \tfrac{1}{4}\arccot(2)\bigr]</math>
|}

By tangential substraction that result appears:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] \oplus R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \Phi^{-1} \ominus \tan\bigl[2\arctan(\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{5} - \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} + 4\sqrt{5}} + \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} - 4\sqrt{5}}\,) - \tfrac{1}{4}\pi \bigr] </math>

{| class = "wikitable"
|<math>R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\tfrac{1}{4}\arccot(- 2) - \arctan(\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{5} - \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} + 4\sqrt{5}} + \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} - 4\sqrt{5}}\,)\bigr]</math>
|}

In an alternative solution way we use the theorem for the squared nome:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^2 R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^{-1}\oplus R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^2 = 1 </math>

:<math> \bigl\{R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^2 R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^{-1} + 1\bigr\}\bigl\{R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^2 + 1\bigr\} = 2 </math>

Now the reflection theorem is taken again:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \Phi^{-1} \ominus R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] </math>

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-2\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \frac{1 - \Phi R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]}{\Phi + R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]} </math>

The insertion of the last mentioned expression into the squared nome theorem gives that equation:

:<math> \biggl\{R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^2 \frac{\Phi + R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]}{1 - \Phi R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]} + 1\biggr\}\biggl\langle R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] \frac{\bigl\{1 - \Phi R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]\bigr\}^2}{\bigl\{\Phi + R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]\bigr\}^2} + 1\biggr\rangle = 2 </math>

Erasing the denominators gives an equation of sixth degree:

:<math> R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^6 + 2\,\Phi^{-2} R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^5 - \sqrt{5}\,\Phi^{-1} R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^4 + </math>

:<math> + 2\,\sqrt{5}\,\Phi R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^3 + \sqrt{5}\,\Phi^{-1} R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr]^2 + 2\,\Phi^{-2} R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] - 1 = 0 </math>

The solution of this equation is the already mentioned solution:

:<math>R\bigl[\exp(-\sqrt{2}\,\pi)\bigr] = \tan\bigl[\arctan(\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{5} - \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} + 4\sqrt{5}} + \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{6\sqrt{30} - 4\sqrt{5}}\,) - \tfrac{1}{4}\arccot(2)\bigr]</math>

==Relation to modular forms==

<math>R(q)</math> can be related to the [[Dedekind eta function]], a [[modular form]] of weight 1/2, as,<ref>Duke, W. "Continued Fractions and Modular Functions", https://www.math.ucla.edu/~wdduke/preprints/bams4.pdf</ref>

:<math>\frac{1}{R(q)}-R(q) = \frac{\eta(\frac{\tau}{5})}{\eta(5\tau)}+1</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{R^5(q)}-R^5(q) = \left[\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(5\tau)}\right]^6+11</math>

The Rogers-Ramanujan continued fraction can also be expressed in terms of the [[Theta_function#Auxiliary_functions|Jacobi theta functions]]. Recall the notation,

:<math>\begin{align}
\vartheta_{10}(0;\tau)&=\theta_2(q)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty q^{(n+1/2)^2}\\
\vartheta_{00}(0;\tau)&=\theta_3(q)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty q^{n^2}\\
\vartheta_{01}(0;\tau)&=\theta_4(q)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty (-1)^n q^{n^2}
\end{align}</math>

The notation <math>\theta_n</math> is slightly easier to remember since <math>\theta_2^4+\theta_4^4 =\theta_3^4</math>, with even subscripts on the LHS. Thus,

: <math>R(x) = \tan\biggl\{\frac{1}{2}\arccot\biggl[\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\theta_{4}(x^{1/5})[5\,\theta_{4}(x^5)^2 - \theta_{4}(x)^2]}{2\,\theta_{4}(x^5)[\theta_{4}(x)^2 - \theta_{4}(x^{1/5})^2]}\biggr]\biggr\}</math>
: <math>R(x) = \tan\biggl\{\frac{1}{2}\arccot\biggl[\frac{1}{2}+\bigg(\frac{\theta_2(x^{1/10})\,\theta_3(x^{1/10})\,\theta_4(x^{1/10})}{2^3\,\theta_2(x^{5/2})\,\theta_3(x^{5/2})\,\theta_4(x^{5/2})}\bigg)^{1/3}\biggr]\biggr\}</math>
: <math>R(x) = \tan\biggl\{\frac{1}{2}\arctan\biggl[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\theta_4(x)^2}{2\,\theta_4(x^5)^2}\biggr]\biggr\}^{1/5}\times\tan\biggl\{\frac{1}{2}\arccot\biggl[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\theta_4(x)^2}{2\,\theta_4(x^5)^2}\biggr]\biggr\}^{2/5}</math>
: <math>R(x) = \tan\biggl\{\frac{1}{2}\arctan\biggl[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\theta_4(x^{1/2})^2}{2\,\theta_4(x^{5/2})^2}\biggr]\biggr\}^{2/5}\times\cot\biggl\{\frac{1}{2}\arccot\biggl[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\theta_4(x^{1/2})^2}{2\,\theta_4(x^{5/2})^2}\biggr]\biggr\}^{1/5}</math>

Note, however, that theta functions normally use the [[nome (mathematics)|nome]] {{math|''q'' {{=}} ''e''<sup>''iπτ''</sup>}}, while the [[Dedekind eta function]] uses the ''square'' of the nome {{math|''q'' {{=}} ''e''<sup>''2iπτ''</sup>}}, thus the variable ''x'' has been employed instead to maintain consistency between all functions. For example, let <math>\tau = \sqrt{-1}</math> so <math>x = e^{-\pi}</math>. Plugging this into the theta functions, one gets the same value for all three ''R''(''x'') formulas which is the correct evaluation of the continued fraction given previously,

:<math>R\big(e^{-\pi}\big) = \frac{1}{2}\varphi\,(\sqrt{5}-\varphi^{3/2})(\sqrt[4]{5}+\varphi^{3/2}) = 0.511428\dots</math>

One can also define the [https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Nome.htm elliptic nome],

:<math>q(k) = \exp\big[-\pi K(\sqrt{1-k^2})/K(k)\big]</math>

The small letter ''k'' describes the elliptic modulus and the big letter ''K'' describes the complete [[elliptic integral]] of the first kind. The continued fraction can then be also expressed by the [[Jacobi elliptic functions]] as follows:

:<math>R\big(q(k)\big) = \tan \biggl\{\frac{1}{2}\arctan y\biggr\}^{1/5} \tan \biggl\{\frac{1}{2}\arccot y \biggr\}^{2/5} =\left\{\frac{\sqrt{y^2+1}-1}{y}\right\}^{1/5} \left\{y\left[\sqrt{\frac{1}{y^2}+1}-1\right]\right\}^{2/5}</math>

with

:<math>y=\frac{2k^2\,\text{sn}[\tfrac{2}{5}K(k);k]^2\,\text{sn}[\tfrac{4}{5}K(k);k]^2}{5-k^2\,\text{sn}[\tfrac{2}{5}K(k);k]^2\,\text{sn}[\tfrac{4}{5}K(k);k]^2}.</math>

==Relation to j-function==

One formula involving the [[j-invariant|j-function]] and the [[Dedekind eta function]] is this:

:<math>j(\tau) = \frac{(x^2+10x+5)^3}{x}</math>

where <math>x = \left[\frac{\sqrt{5}\,\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(\tau)}\right]^6.\,</math> Since also,

:<math>\frac{1}{R^5(q)}-R^5(q) = \left[\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(5\tau)}\right]^6+11</math>

Eliminating the eta quotient <math>x</math> between the two equations, one can then express ''j''(''τ'') in terms of <math>r =R(q)</math> as,

:<math>
\begin{align}
& j(\tau) = -\frac{(r^{20}-228r^{15}+494r^{10}+228r^5+1)^3}{r^5(r^{10}+11r^5-1)^5} \\[6pt]
& j(\tau)-1728 = -\frac{(r^{30}+ 522r^{25}- 10005 r^{20}- 10005 r^{10}- 522 r^5 + 1)^2}{r^5(r^{10}+ 11 r^5-1)^5}
\end{align}
</math>

where the [[numerator]] and [[denominator]] are polynomial invariants of the [[icosahedron]].  Using the [[modular equation]] between <math>R(q)</math> and <math>R(q^5)</math>, one finds that,

:<math>
\begin{align}
& j(5\tau) = -\frac{(r^{20}+12r^{15}+14r^{10}-12r^5+1)^3}{r^{25}(r^{10}+11r^5-1)} \\[6pt]
& j(5\tau)-1728 = -\frac{(r^{30}+18r^{25}+75r^{20}+75r^{10}-18r^5+1)^2}{r^{25}(r^{10}+11r^5-1)}
\end{align}
</math>

Let <math>z=r^5-\frac{1}{r^5}</math>, then <math>j(5\tau) = -\frac{ \left( z^2 + 12z + 16 \right)^3}{z+11}</math>

where

: <math>
\begin{align}
& z_\infty = -\left[\frac{\sqrt{5}\,\eta(25\tau)}{\eta(5\tau)}\right]^6-11,\ z_0=-\left[ \frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(5\tau)} \right]^6-11,\ z_1=\left[\frac{\eta(\frac{5\tau+2}{5})}{\eta(5\tau)}\right]^6-11, \\[6pt]
& z_2=-\left[\frac{\eta(\frac{5\tau+4}{5})}{\eta(5\tau)}\right]^6-11,\  z_3=\left[\frac{\eta(\frac{5\tau+6}{5})}{\eta(5\tau)}\right]^6-11,\ z_4=-\left[ \frac{\eta(\frac{5\tau+8}{5})}{\eta(5\tau)}\right]^6-11
\end{align}
</math>

which in fact is the j-invariant of the [[elliptic curve]],

:<math>y^2+(1+r^5)xy+r^5y=x^3+r^5x^2</math>

parameterized by the non-cusp points of the [[Modular curve#Examples|modular curve]] <math>X_1(5)</math>.

==Functional equation==

For convenience, one can also use the notation <math>r(\tau) = R(q)</math> when ''q'' = e<sup>2πiτ</sup>. While other modular functions like the j-invariant satisfies,

:<math>j(-\tfrac{1}{\tau}) = j(\tau)</math>

and the Dedekind eta function has,

:<math>\eta(-\tfrac{1}{\tau}) =\sqrt{-i\tau}\, \eta(\tau)</math>

the [[functional equation]] of the Rogers–Ramanujan continued fraction involves<ref>Duke, W. "Continued Fractions and Modular Functions" (p.9)</ref> the [[golden ratio]] <math>\varphi</math>,

:<math>r(-\tfrac{1}{\tau}) = \frac{1-\varphi\,r(\tau)}{\varphi+r(\tau)}</math>

Incidentally,

:<math>r(\tfrac{7+i}{10}) = i</math>

==Modular equations==

There are modular equations between <math>R(q)</math> and <math>R(q^n)</math>. Elegant ones for small [[prime number|prime]] ''n'' are as follows.<ref>Berndt, B. et al. "The Rogers–Ramanujan Continued Fraction", http://www.math.uiuc.edu/~berndt/articles/rrcf.pdf</ref>

For <math>n = 2</math>, let <math>u=R(q)</math> and <math>v=R(q^2)</math>, then <math>v-u^2 = (v+u^2)uv^2.</math>

For <math>n = 3</math>, let <math>u=R(q)</math> and <math>v=R(q^3)</math>, then <math>(v-u^3)(1+uv^3) = 3u^2v^2.</math>

For <math>n = 5</math>, let <math>u=R(q)</math> and <math>v=R(q^5)</math>, then <math>v(v^4-3v^3+4v^2-2v+1)=(v^4+2v^3+4v^2+3v+1)u^5.</math>

Or equivalently for <math>n = 5</math>, let <math>u=R(q)</math> and <math>v=R(q^5)</math> and <math>\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}2</math>, then <math>u^5 = \frac{v\,(v^2-\varphi^2v+\varphi^2)(v^2-\varphi^{-2}v+\varphi^{-2})}{(v^2+v+\varphi^2)(v^2+v+\varphi^{-2})}.</math>

For <math>n = 11</math>, let <math>u=R(q)</math> and <math>v=R(q^{11})</math>, then <math>uv(u^{10}+11u^5-1)(v^{10}+11v^5-1) = (u-v)^{12}.</math>

Regarding <math>n = 5</math>, note that <math>v^{10}+11v^5-1=(v^2+v-1)(v^4-3v^3+4v^2-2v+1)(v^4+2v^3+4v^2+3v+1).</math>

==Other results==

Ramanujan found many other interesting results regarding <math>R(q)</math>.<ref>Berndt, B. et al. "The Rogers–Ramanujan Continued Fraction"</ref> Let <math>a,b\in\mathbb{R}^+</math>, and <math>\varphi</math> as the [[golden ratio]].

If <math>ab=\pi^2</math> then,

:<math>\bigl[R(e^{-2a})+\varphi\bigl]\bigl[R(e^{-2b})+\varphi\bigr]=\sqrt{5}\,\varphi.</math>

If <math>5ab=\pi^2</math> then,

:<math>\bigl[R^5(e^{-2a})+\varphi^5\bigl]\bigl[R^5(e^{-2b})+\varphi^5\bigr]=5\sqrt{5}\,\varphi^5.</math>

The powers of <math>R(q)</math> also can be expressed in unusual ways. For its [[Cube (algebra)|cube]],

:<math>R^3(q) = \frac{\alpha}{\beta}</math>

where

:<math>\alpha=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{q^{2n}}{1-q^{5n+2}}-\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{q^{3n+1}}{1-q^{5n+3}},</math>
:<math>\beta=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{q^n}{1-q^{5n+1}}-\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{q^{4n+3}}{1-q^{5n+4}}.</math>

For its fifth power, let <math>w=R(q)R^2(q^2)</math>, then,

:<math>R^5(q) = w\left(\frac{1-w}{1+w}\right)^2,\;\; R^5(q^2) = w^2\left(\frac{1+w}{1-w} \right)</math>

== Quintic equations ==

The general [[Quintic function|quintic equation]] in Bring-Jerrard form:

:<math>x^5 - 5x - 4a = 0</math>

for every real value <math>a > 1</math> can be solved in terms of Rogers-Ramanujan continued fraction <math>R(q)</math> and the elliptic nome

:<math>q(k) = \exp\big[-\pi K(\sqrt{1-k^2})/K(k)\big].</math>

To solve this quintic, the elliptic modulus must first be determined as

:<math>k = \tan[\tfrac{1}{4}\pi - \tfrac{1}{4}\arccsc(a^2)]. </math>

Then the real solution is

:<math>\begin{align}x&= \frac{2 - \bigl\{1 - R[q(k)]\bigr\}\bigl\{1+R[q(k)^2]\bigr\}}{\sqrt{R[q(k)]\,R[q(k)^2]}\,\sqrt[4]{4\cot\langle 4\arctan\{S\}\rangle - 3}}\\&= \frac{2 - \bigl\{1 - R[q(k)]\bigr\}\bigl\{1+R[q(k)^2]\bigr\}}{\sqrt{R[q(k)]R[q(k)^2]}\,\sqrt[4]{\frac{2}{S-1}+\frac{2}{S+1}+\frac{1}{S}-S-3}}. \end{align}</math>

where <math>S=R[q(k)]\,R^2[q(k)^2].</math>. Recall in the previous section the 5th power of <math>R(q)</math> can be expressed by <math>S</math>:

:<math>R^5[q(k)] = S\left(\frac{1-S}{1+S}\right)^2</math>

=== Example 1 ===

:<math>x^5 - x - 1 = 0</math>

Transform to,

:<math>(\sqrt[4]{5}x)^5 - 5(\sqrt[4]{5}x) - 4(\tfrac{5}{4}\sqrt[4]{5}) = 0</math>

thus,

:<math>a = \tfrac{5}{4}\sqrt[4]{5} </math>

:<math>k = \tan[\tfrac{1}{4}\pi - \tfrac{1}{4}\arccsc(a^2)] = \tfrac{5^{5/4}+\sqrt{25\sqrt{5}-16}}{5^{5/4}+\sqrt{25\sqrt{5}+16}}</math>

:<math>q(k) = 0.0851414716\dots </math>

:<math>R[q(k)] = 0.5633613184\dots </math>

:<math>R[q(k)^2] = 0.3706122329\dots </math>

and the solution is:

:<math>x = \frac{2 - \bigl\{1 - R[q(k)]\bigr\}\bigl\{1+R[q(k)^2]\bigr\}}{\sqrt{R[q(k)]\,R[q(k)^2]}\,\sqrt[4]{20\cot\langle 4\arctan\{R[q(k)]\,R[q(k)^2]^2\}\rangle - 15}} = 1.167303978\dots</math>

and can not be represented by elementary root expressions.

=== Example 2 ===

:<math>x^5 - 5x - 4\Bigl(\sqrt[4]{\tfrac{81}{32}}\Bigr) = 0</math>

thus,

:<math>a = \sqrt[4]{\tfrac{81}{32}} </math>

Given the more familiar continued fractions with closed-forms,

:<math>r_1 = R\big(e^{-\pi}\big) = \tfrac{1}{2}\varphi\,(\sqrt{5}-\varphi^{3/2})(\sqrt[4]{5}+\varphi^{3/2}) = 0.511428\dots </math>

:<math>r_2 = R\big(e^{-2\pi}\big) = \sqrt[4]{5}\,\varphi^{1/2}-\varphi = 0.284079\dots</math>

:<math>r_4 = R\big(e^{-4\pi}\big) = \tfrac{1}{2}\varphi\,(\sqrt{5}-\varphi^{3/2})(-\sqrt[4]{5}+\varphi^{3/2}) = 0.081002\dots</math>

with golden ratio <math>\varphi = \tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}</math> and the solution simplifies to

:<math>\begin{align}x
&= \sqrt[4]{5}\,\frac{2 - \bigl\{1 - r_1\bigr\}\bigl\{1+r_2\bigr\}}{\sqrt{r_1\,r_2}\,\sqrt[4]{20\cot\langle 4\arctan\{r_1\,r_2^2\}\rangle - 15}}\\[6pt]
&= \sqrt[4]{5}\,\frac{2 - \bigl\{1 - r_2\bigr\}\bigl\{1+r_4\bigr\}}{\sqrt{r_2\,r_4}\,\sqrt[4]{20\cot\langle 4\arctan\{r_2\,r_4^2\}\rangle - 15}}\\[6pt]
&= \sqrt[4]{8} = 1.681792\dots\end{align}</math>
